{"slug": "how-to-launch-a-startup-landing-page", "title": "How to Launch a Startup Landing Page (2026 Guide)", "metaTitle": "How to Launch a Startup Landing Page (2026 Guide)", "metaDescription": "A practical walkthrough for validating a startup idea with a real landing page before you build the product, plus how to launch one fast with Kodely.", "targetKeyword": "how to launch a startup landing page", "category": "Guides", "bodyHtml": "

Most startups build the product before they know anyone wants it. A landing page flips that order. It costs you an afternoon instead of a month, and it tells you whether the idea is worth the month. This guide walks through what to put on that page, an example prompt you can copy, and how to get it live today.

Why a landing page comes before the product

A landing page is the cheapest experiment you can run. Before you write a line of backend code, hire a designer, or commit to a tech stack, you can put your value proposition in front of real people and watch what they do with it. Do they read past the headline? Do they click the call to action? Do they hand over an email address for something that does not exist yet?

That signal is worth more than a friend telling you your idea sounds cool. It is worth more than a spreadsheet of assumptions. It is an actual behavior, from an actual stranger, measured before you have spent real money building anything. If nobody bites, you saved yourself months. If people do, you now have a list of interested humans to talk to while you build.

What a startup landing page actually needs

A validation page is not a full marketing site. It does not need a blog, a pricing table with six tiers, or a careers page. It needs to do one job well: convince a stranger in fifteen seconds that this is for them, then ask for a small commitment. Strip it down to these pieces:

  • A clear value proposition. One sentence, above the fold, that says what the product does and who it is for. No jargon, no vague promises.
  • The problem you solve. A short section that names the pain point in language your visitor already uses. This is where people recognize themselves.
  • A single call to action. Early access, join the waitlist, get notified at launch — pick one goal and repeat it, not three competing buttons.
  • Just enough proof. A short list of features or benefits, maybe a line about who is building it. Enough to build trust, not so much that it reads like a finished product pitch.

Everything else is noise at this stage. Testimonials you do not have yet, an FAQ for questions nobody has asked, a pricing page for a product that does not exist — cut it. The page exists to test one hypothesis, not to look impressive.

The honest note on email capture

Most validation pages end with an email form: enter your address, get notified when we launch. That form is easy to design and easy to get wrong, so here is the honest version of how it works with Kodely.

Kodely will build you a real, working form UI — input field, validation state, submit button, confirmation message, all of it styled and functional in the browser. What it will not do is store or process those emails on a backend, because Kodely does not generate backend logic, databases, or auth. There is nowhere on the Kodely side for those addresses to go.

That is fine, and it is normal for this stage. The fix is to connect the form to a dedicated email capture tool built for exactly this job — something like a waitlist or newsletter service that gives you a form endpoint or embed code. You wire that endpoint into the form Kodely built, and now submissions actually land somewhere you can read them. The page still comes together in one chat session; you are just plugging in one small piece from outside.

A real example prompt

Here is a prompt you could give Kodely to generate a first draft of a validation page for a fictional product:

Example prompt: Build a one-page startup landing site for a product called Fernway, a tool that turns messy meeting notes into structured follow-up tasks automatically. Include a hero section with a headline, subheadline, and an email signup form for early access. Add a section explaining the problem — teams lose action items because nobody writes clean notes. Add a three-item feature list: auto-detects tasks, assigns owners, syncs to your task tool. Use a clean, modern layout with a single accent color and generous whitespace. End with a repeated call to action to join the waitlist.

You can watch the real components come together in the live preview as Kodely builds them, then keep refining in chat — swap the copy, change the accent color, add a section — until it matches what you had in mind.

How to launch it fast with Kodely

The whole loop happens in one place. You describe the page in plain English, and Kodely generates a real Vite plus React 19 and TypeScript app styled with Tailwind CSS v4 — actual component files, not a static mockup. You watch it render live as it is built, and if a generation fails to compile, you are not charged for it.

When it looks right, click Publish and the page goes live on a free yourname.kodely.site URL immediately, with an automatic scan for any leaked secrets before it goes public. Every successful generation is saved as a checkpoint, so if an edit takes the page somewhere you do not like, rolling back is free and instant. You can also open the code view to see and copy the actual source files at any point.

Signing up gives you 750 free credits, no credit card required, which is comfortably enough to build and publish a landing page like this one.

How to iterate once you start getting signups and feedback

Once the page is live and people start signing up, treat every batch of signups as new information. Watch which headline gets more clicks by testing a variant. Read any replies or comments you get and fold the language people use into your copy — real customer words convert better than what you assumed they would say. If a section is not getting attention, cut it. If a feature you did not emphasize keeps coming up, promote it higher on the page.

Each of these is a small chat message to Kodely: change the headline, remove the middle section, reorder the feature list. It edits the real components directly, and you get a new checkpoint each time, so testing ideas costs you nothing but a few minutes.

FAQ

Do I need to know how to code to build this? No. You describe the page in chat and Kodely generates the real components for you. You can view and copy the underlying code if you want to, but it is not required.

Can I use my own domain? Not yet. Published pages live on a free yourname.kodely.site subdomain today.

Will this build my actual product? No, and it should not try to. This builds the marketing page — the thing you use to validate demand and capture interest. It does not generate a backend, database, authentication, or payments. Once you have validated the idea, that becomes a separate build.

What happens to the emails people submit? The form itself is real and functional in the browser, but Kodely has no backend to store submissions. Connect the form to a dedicated email capture or waitlist tool to actually collect and manage those addresses.

Can I download the code and host it elsewhere? Not currently. There is no zip export yet — publishing through Kodely to your kodely.site subdomain is the way to get it live today.

Ready to see your idea as a real page instead of a note in your notes app? Do it now on Kodely, free — no credit card required.
